doc.title: Stanley Kay interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 18, 2001

title: How the business changed after the band era
summary: Kay talks about vocalists, rock and roll and the end of dancing, then Buddy's complexity.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Good statement. How did the business change during the war years?

Well when the band thing was over, you know, I caught some of the good part of it. When the business changed they went into vocalists, which was great, because the vocalist still accompanied the bands. You know, Ella Fitzgerald, one of the greatest of all time, and I got to play with her. I subbed in Buddy Morrow’s band. And I took the gig, I had three days off, because I loved the way Buddy played trombone and I wanted to hear her sing. So I played for three days. The business changed I think, and due respect, when the rock & roll, whatever the name of those groups, the Chandeliers, the Lamps the Trees, the I don’t know the Beds. When they came in, that did it. You know they had this new thing. Because what they do, they don’t really — they listen — in my opinion, and I don’t argue with success or whoever you like. I thought Eminem was a candy.

You know, but if the kids like that, that’s their time. You know I can’t say don’t like it, you like it, like it. We didn’t have all wonderful things in our time too. So it becomes opinion. What do you like? What do you like? And it changed because of that. Then the promoters concentrated on that. On making — no more dancing, that started it you know. And Buddy [Rich], toward later on, he wouldn’t play for dancing. He had a concert band. He would not play for dancing later on. But that was his choice. But he was so phenomenal, I mean he would have been 82 on September 30th he would have been 82. And I really believe this, really in my heart. If he was alive today he would have played the same way that he did. He may have got a little more tired, but look out. I used to tell him, we’d talk. And you know you have your ups and downs financially. I’d have five dollars in my pocket and I’d give him two fifty and I’d take two fifty and we’d take the train to Brooklyn. I’d stay over at his house sometimes. And I used to say to him you know, “God said — Zen, Buddah, whoever you believe in — is going to put someone on this earth to do this thing better than anyone else, and he chose you and you don’t know what to do with it.” Because of his complexities.
